lines.trans: Have you completely lost your mind?
I lay down for five minutes.
You cannot sleep in the kitchen!
I could not sleep all night.
Why didn't you sleep at night?
I am not used to Moscow yet.
Quickly get up and wash dishes!

meanings.note: International noun in '-ция' (from Latin '-tio'), feminine declension. Common feminine noun meaning 'acclimatization' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: What on earth kind of acclimatization?!

meanings.note: the comparative 'быстрее', often as an order
the comparative 'быстрее', often as an order

examples.text: Виталик, почему мы так медленно едем? Быстрее!
examples.trans: Vitalik, why are we going so slowly? Faster!

examples.text: Давай работай быстрее, гости уже давно ждут заказ!
examples.trans: Come on, work faster, the guests have been waiting for their order for a long time!

meanings.note: Russian determiner/pronoun ('all') agreeing in gender, number, and case with the noun phrase it specifies.
Secondary conversational sense ('everything') (neuter всё) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('everyone') (plural все) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

вставать.gloss: to get up, to stand up

meanings.note: Prefix 'вс-' ('up') marks upward or sudden onset of action (stem 'тавать'). Used in Russian as an imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to get up', forming an aspectual pair with 'встать'.
Secondary conversational sense ('to stand up') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Come on, Tuzik, let's get up!
I get up at seven in the morning.
Come on, Tuzik, let's get up!

meanings.note: Declinable feminine noun meaning 'meeting', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.
Secondary conversational sense ('see you') (in 'до встречи' = until we meet) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Решается ваш вопрос, Клавдия Викторовна! Вы не видите, у меня встреча?
examples.trans: Your question is being sorted out, Klavdia Viktorovna! Can't you see I have a meeting?

meanings.note: Russian preposition meaning 'until' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.
Secondary conversational sense ('goodbye') used in spoken Russian dialogue.
in threats: ты ещё увидишь = you'll see
Secondary conversational sense ('still, yet') used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('even (with comparatives)') (ещё больше = even more) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: У тебя же есть ещё. Дай хоть одну.
examples.trans: But you've still got some. Give me just one.

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'here'.
emphasis: вот поэтому ты и... = that's exactly why you...

examples.trans: I was born and grew up here.

examples.text: Спасибо, спасибо! Как вы все знаете, я родился и вырос в Синеозерске.
examples.trans: Thank you, thank you! As you all know, I was born and grew up in Sineozersk.

meanings.note: Russian preposition meaning 'to' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.

examples.trans: There's someone here to see you.

examples.text: Аркадий Борисович, извините, тут к вам человек.
examples.trans: Arkady Borisovich, I'm sorry, there's a man here to see you.

meanings.note: Russian determiner/pronoun ('what') agreeing in gender, number, and case with the noun phrase it specifies.
in exclamations: какой грязный! = how dirty!

examples.text: Смотрите, какой у нас грязный унитаз!
examples.trans: Look, how dirty our toilet is!

meanings.note: Entered Russian via Polish 'kuchnia' and Middle High German 'küchen', ultimately from Late Latin 'coquina' (from 'coquere', to cook).
Secondary conversational sense ('cuisine, cooking') (русская кухня = Russian cuisine) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Three rooms and a big kitchen.
And the kitchen is over there.

meanings.note: Common feminine noun meaning 'minute' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: I'll be there in ten minutes.

examples.text: Ладно, будь там. Через десять минут буду.
examples.trans: All right, stay there. I'll be there in ten minutes.

meanings.note: Russian determiner/pronoun ('my') agreeing in gender, number, and case with the noun phrase it specifies.
praise, said to a man, woman or child
Secondary conversational sense ('a fine young man') (old-fashioned) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: I see, I see, you're a hero. Well done.

examples.text: Молодец, Макс, ты сегодня отлично справился с горячим цехом!
examples.trans: Well done, Max, you handled the hot station brilliantly today!

meanings.note: Russian imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'can', forming an aspectual pair with 'смочь'; conjugates for person and number in the present/future and agrees in gender in the past tense.

examples.text: Этого не может быть. Это наша история.
examples.trans: That can't be. It's our history.

meanings.note: Russian imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to wash', forming an aspectual pair with 'помыть'; conjugates for person and number in the present/future and agrees in gender in the past tense.

examples.text: Юля, встала и пошла мыть посуду!
examples.trans: Yulia, get up and go wash the dishes!

examples.text: Пока ещё на мои деньги куплен! Встала и мыть посуду, шагом марш!
examples.trans: It's still bought with my money! Get up and wash the dishes, forward march!

meanings.note: Russian preposition meaning 'on' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.
Secondary conversational sense ('onto, to; for') (+ accusative: на второй срок) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: The programme is on the website.
He is running for a second term.

examples.text: Я очень люблю наш город. Поэтому я иду на второй срок.
examples.trans: I love our town very much. That's why I'm running for a second term.

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'probably'.

examples.trans: Well, probably somewhere in the archive.
He has probably already come home.

examples.text: Наверное, что-то серьёзное у вас. Девочка уже две недели лежит в областной клинике!
examples.trans: It must be something serious for you. The girl has been lying in the regional clinic for two weeks already!

meanings.note: goes right before the word it negates

нельзя.gloss: it is not allowed; one can't

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'it is not allowed'.
Secondary conversational sense ('impossible, can't') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Not allowed? All right, I'll go and do my homework.

meanings.note: ночью = at night; спокойной ночи = good night

examples.text: Ну что, Аркаша? Наступила ночь, просыпается мафия.
examples.trans: So, Arkasha? Night has fallen, the mafia wakes up.

meanings.note: playful derogatory nickname used by Chef Barinov for Max

examples.trans: Runt, are you still standing here?
The chef often called the newcomer a runt.

examples.text: Огузок, ты официально принят в штат нашего ресторана!
examples.trans: Rump, you are officially hired onto our restaurant staff!

meanings.note: Conversational Russian particle ('please') that adds modal nuance, emphasis, or discourse tone in spoken dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('you're welcome') (answer to thanks) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('here you are') (handing something over) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

meanings.en: dishes, plates and cups, tableware (collective singular)
meanings.note: Declinable feminine noun meaning 'dishes', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.

examples.trans: Get up and go wash the dishes!
Clean tableware is on the table.

examples.text: Юля, встала и пошла мыть посуду!
examples.trans: Yulia, get up and go wash the dishes!

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'why'.

examples.trans: Why are we going so slowly?

examples.text: Виталик, почему мы так медленно едем? Быстрее!
examples.trans: Vitalik, why are we going so slowly? Faster!

meanings.en: to get used to, become accustomed
meanings.note: Prefix 'при-' indicates approaching, attachment, or slight degree of action (stem 'выкнуть'). Used in Russian as an perfective verb focusing on a single completed action or result meaning 'to get used to'.

examples.text: Я ещё не привык к Москве.
examples.trans: I am not used to Moscow yet.

examples.text: Ты уже привык к жизни в Москве?
examples.trans: Have you already gotten used to life in Moscow?
I got used to working by the law.

meanings.en: to lie down for a short rest
meanings.note: Prefix 'при-' indicates approaching, attachment, or slight degree of action (stem 'лечь'). Used in Russian as an perfective verb focusing on a single completed action or result meaning 'to lie down'.

examples.trans: I lay down for five minutes.

examples.text: Я просто прилёг на пять минут.
examples.trans: I simply lay down for five minutes.

meanings.note: Prefix 'про-' indicates movement through, completion, or missing the mark (stem 'стить'). Used in Russian as an perfective verb focusing on a single completed action or result meaning 'to forgive', forming an aspectual pair with 'прощать'.
Secondary conversational sense ('excuse me, sorry') (imperative: прости / простите) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Russian numeral ('five') that declines for case and governs case agreement on the counted noun.

examples.text: Мы же только начинаем. Через месяц будет пять тысяч.
examples.trans: But we're only just starting. In a month there'll be five thousand.

meanings.note: + instrumental; со before some consonant clusters: со всеми

examples.trans: Share it all equally with everyone, understand?

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'quite'.
Secondary conversational sense ('not at all') (совсем не) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Я совсем не это хочу сказать.
examples.trans: That's not what I mean at all.

examples.text: Нет, Вика, я совсем не это хочу сказать.
examples.trans: No, Vika, that's not what I mean at all.

сойти.gloss: to get off; to go mad

meanings.en: to get off, to step down
meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'ойти'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to get off; (с ума) to go mad', paired with 'сходить'.

meanings.en: to go mad, to lose one's mind
meanings.note: Secondary conversational sense ('to go mad, to lose one's mind') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: What, have I lost my mind?

examples.text: Позвонить Третьякову? Я что, с ума сошёл?
examples.trans: Call Tretyakov? What, have I lost my mind?

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'пать'). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to sleep', paired with 'поспать'.

examples.text: Ладно, утром позвоню ей. Поехали спать.
examples.trans: All right, I'll call her in the morning. Let's go to sleep.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronoun ('you') whose case form reflects its grammatical role in the clause.
Secondary conversational sense ('other forms:  (gen/acc),  (dat),  (instr),  (prep)') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Dad, did you bring any gum?

meanings.note: уже четыре года = for four years now

examples.text: Я уже четыре года работаю мэром.
examples.trans: I've been mayor for four years now.

meanings.note: сойти с ума = to go mad, lose one's mind

examples.text: Позвонить Третьякову? Я что, с ума сошёл?
examples.trans: Call Tretyakov? What, have I lost my mind?

meanings.note: Prefix 'у-' marks departure, removal, or successful completion (stem 'снуть'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to fall asleep', paired with 'засыпать'.

examples.trans: He will fall asleep quickly after the injection.

examples.text: Он быстро уснёт после этого сильного препарата?
examples.trans: Will he fall asleep quickly after this strong medication?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronoun ('what') whose case form reflects its grammatical role in the clause.
Secondary conversational sense ('that') (conjunction) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('? = well?') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Привет! Смотри, что у меня есть.

meanings.note: pointing at a thing or a situation; 'это' + noun = 'this is ...'
points at something: это моё = that's mine
Secondary conversational sense ('is') (linking word: главное — это народ) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('other forms:') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: And this is for you. A toy car!

meanings.note: меня = me (genitive/accusative), мне = to me (dative)
Secondary conversational sense ('other forms:  (gen/acc),  (dat),  (instr),  (prep)') used in spoken Russian dialogue.
